text: Hsien Chung (or Hsien-Chung or Hsien-chung) Wang (王宪钟 Wang Xian Zhong; 18 April 1918 in Beijing – 25 June 1978 in New York City) was a Chinese-American mathematician specializing in differential geometry, Lie groups, and algebraic topology. Born into a family from Shandong Province with a history of producing distinguished scholars over several generations, Wang studied at Nankai High School in Tianjin, where he achieved an outstanding academic record. In 1936, he enrolled at Tsing Hua University in Beijing. On 7 July 1937, Japanese and Chinese troops clashed near Peking; by late July, further fighting erupted, and the Japanese captured Peking and Tientsin. Tsing Hua University was relocated to Southwest China, where it was merged with Nankai and Peking universities. Wang traveled to the new university location and resumed his studies, during which he switched to mathematics. He graduated in 1941 and began studying under S S Chern, earning a master's degree in 1944 and starting teaching at a school. After one year, he received a British Council Scholarship to continue his studies in England, where he studied under Newman at Manchester and obtained a Ph.D. in 1948. Following his Ph.D., Wang moved to the United States, where he initially served as a lecturer at Louisiana State University. Despite a heavy teaching load, he remained active and successful in research, earning recognition through a visiting membership at the Institute of Advanced Study at Princeton from 1951 to 1952. He was highly esteemed by the institute's faculty and was invited back for visits in 1954–55, 1961–62, and 1965. His work gained widespread recognition in the early 1950s. He held academic positions at the Alabama Polytechnic Institute, the University of Washington, Columbia University, and Northwestern University. In 1966, he accepted a professorship at Cornell, where he became one of the most respected and distinguished members of the faculty until his sudden death from leukemia. Wang was an Invited Speaker at the International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) in 1958 in Edinburgh. He was a Guggenheim Fellow for the academic year 1960–1961. The Wang sequence, used in algebraic topology, is named in his honor. Wang married in 1956 and had three daughters. His doctoral student includes J. Stephen Halperin.
